title: Exact exponential-time equivalence for nonnegative Boolean Max-CSP
formal: Does the following extension of the source’s degree-based classification hold? For every fixed finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) that is neither 0-valid, 1-valid, nor 2-monotone, let \(d=\deg (\Gamma )\). For every fixed real \(\alpha >1\), if Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) has an exact deterministic algorithm running in \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\) time for every fixed constant \(c\ge 1\), must Max d-CNF-SAT with nonnegative integer weights of total weight at most \(n^{c}\) also have an exact deterministic \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for every fixed \(c\ge 1\)? The same base \(\alpha\) is required. Algorithms and polynomial factors may depend on \(\Gamma ,\alpha ,c\). This formulates the conclusion’s speedup question as extending Theorem 6.2 to all NP-hard nonnegative-weight languages; tractable languages are explicitly excluded.
context:
Theorem 6.2 places all degree-d signed-weight languages in the same exact exponential-base class as weighted Max d-CNF-SAT. The forward implication from Max d-CNF-SAT algorithms also covers its nonnegative-weight restrictions.

The same theorem covers nonnegative languages closed under predicate-output negation, \(f\mapsto 1- f\), or under substitution of literals for arguments. An arbitrary NP-hard language need not have either closure.

The source’s additive reductions introduce only \(O(1)\) variables, so \(\alpha ^{n+O(1)}\) preserves \(\alpha\). Its general conversion to nonnegative weights can instead introduce a linear number of variables. That suffices for transferring a polynomial compression exponent but can change an exponential base.

The March 2024 version repeats the nonnegative-weight speedup question after the exponential-time theorem. Its complete compression classification does not itself resolve the exact-time classification.
why: Would show whether the algebraic degree of a Boolean constraint language determines its exact exponential-time complexity even when every constraint has the usual nonnegative weight.
status_note: Checked the conference statement against the March 2024 version of record, including the exact-base quantifiers, all-c convention and tractability dichotomy. Subsequent searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a general resolution. The displayed statement is the NP-hard-language extension of the source’s Theorem 6.2; this editorial interpretation of the shorter conclusion is explicit. Search is not exhaustive.

progress.text: The ESA paper proves the signed-weight and closure-restricted exact-base classification, leaving general nonnegative languages open.
The full TOCT article retains both Theorem 6.2 and the missing nonnegative-weight question.

sentences: A Boolean Max-CSP instance asks for an assignment satisfying constraints of maximum total nonnegative weight.
Each fixed language has a degree defined by the real multilinear polynomials of its predicates.
The question asks whether an exact algorithm with exponential base \(\alpha\) for any NP-hard degree-d language yields the same base for weighted Max d-CNF-SAT.
The known classification allows negative weights or imposes closure properties on the language.
The remaining issue is preserving the exponential base when removing the sign restriction; the 2024 journal article still asks it.

references.authors: Jansen, Bart M. P.; Włodarczyk, Michał

definitions: A Boolean predicate f of arity r is a map \(\{0,1\}\)ʳ→\(\{0,1\}\). A language \(\Gamma\) is a fixed finite set of such predicates, not part of an input instance. An instance \(\Phi\) has variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and weighted applications \((f,(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{r}),w)\), where \(f\in \Gamma\), each \(i_{j}\in [n]\) and w is a nonnegative integer. Indices may repeat. Arguments are variables themselves: constants and negated literals are available only if the corresponding predicate can already be expressed by a member of \(\Gamma\) with variable arguments. The value \(\Phi (x)\) is the sum of weights whose predicate applications evaluate to 1. Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) asks whether \(\max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{n}}\Phi (x)\ge t\) for an input integer t, under the promise that total weight is at most \(n^{c}\). Weights, indices and t use binary encoding; duplicate applications can be combined and zero-weight applications discarded. Trivial thresholds outside the possible objective range are handled during input reading. Polynomial-time normalization is included; equivalently the runtime has an additional input-reading term for a redundantly listed representation. The normalized input has polynomial length for fixed \(\Gamma ,c\). The algorithm must answer every promised instance correctly, and n denotes variables, not clauses, total weight or bit length. For each f there is a unique multilinear real polynomial \(\mathrm{P}_{f}\) agreeing with f on its Boolean cube. Its degree is the largest number of variables in a monomial with nonzero coefficient; \(\deg (\Gamma )=\max _{f\in \Gamma}\deg (\mathrm{P}_{f})\). This is neither maximum predicate arity nor polynomial degree over \(F_{2}\). Constants can be removed with a threshold adjustment. Disregarding constant predicates, a language is 0-valid if every predicate accepts its all-zero input, and 1-valid if every predicate accepts its all-one input. It is 2-monotone if each predicate has a DNF representation with at most two terms, one consisting only of positive variables and one only of negated variables. The excluded three cases are the source’s polynomial-time cases for nonnegative weights; the remaining cases are NP-hard and have \(d\ge 2\). Max d-CNF-SAT is the same threshold maximization problem for disjunctions of at most d literals, with both signs of variables allowed, and nonnegative integer clause weights. Equivalently one may use the source’s d-ary clause language and repeated variables. All complexity statements are worst-case exact running times in an ordinary discrete computation model, up to polynomial factors. The premise is quantified over every fixed polynomial weight bound c; a result for only one small weight range does not supply that premise.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication for every eligible fixed language \(\Gamma\) and every \(\alpha >1\), retaining the same exponential base and the all-c weight convention, or refute it by a language and a rigorously established failure of that implication. A theorem comparing only whether both problems are NP-hard, or comparing compression sizes or exponential rates after a constant-factor increase in variable count, does not establish the stated base-preserving classification.
